issues.legal_issue: A tenant seeking statutory purchase rights is ineligible when the leased land is appurtenant to a building rather than land leased separately from buildings and their appurtenances.
material_facts: In an ejectment suit, the tenant applied for the statutory right to purchase land.
The lease covered an existing substantial building and a much larger surrounding area.
The courts found that, given the property's nature and its use at the time of the lease, the surrounding land was used incidentally to the enjoyment of the building.
The lease's description of the subject matter as land and buildings did not determine whether the land was appurtenant.
issues.conclusion: The land was appurtenant to the building, so the tenant was not entitled to the statutory rights to compensation or purchase.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(1) and 2(2) of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, land does not include buildings, and a building includes its appurtenances. Sections 3 and 9 provide rights to compensation and purchase to qualifying tenants of land; those rights do not apply where the tenancy is of a building with appurtenant land. Whether land is appurtenant is a question of fact, assessed by its extent, nature, situation in relation to the building, and use. The Court applied Maharaja Singh v. State of U.P., [1977] 7 SCC 155, including its explanation that appurtenance involves dependence or an incidental or ancillary relationship to the building's use as a building.

predicates.tenant_seeks_statutory_purchase_in_eject: A tenant facing an ejectment suit applies for a statutory right to purchase land.
predicates.leased_property_includes_building: The property leased includes a building as well as land.
predicates.surrounding_land_used_incidentally_for_b: The surrounding land is used incidentally to the enjoyment and beneficial use of the building.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeks a statutory purchase right in an ejectment proceeding and the leased property includes a building whose surrounding land is used incidentally for it, the tenant is not entitled to that purchase right.

issues.legal_issue: A lease of a building and land is not divisible into separate leases when its terms and the property do not identify a distinct, separately demised area of land.
material_facts: The deed referred jointly to the building and land as the demised premises and provided for a single lease term, renewal, termination, and surrender.
It stated an aggregate monthly rent, although the rent was apportioned between land and building, and required a consolidated advance.
The deed did not provide for separate termination or renewal of the building lease and the land lease.
The deed did not define or delineate an area that could be treated as a separate lease of vacant land.
The deed permitted construction, subletting, and a possible sale option, but the Court regarded these as provisions addressing contingencies during the lease rather than creating separate leases.
issues.conclusion: The deed created one indivisible composite lease of the building and its appurtenant land, not two separate leases.
issues.legal_principle: The lease must be construed as a whole in light of its terms and the nature of the property. Separate rents, permissions to build or sublet, and a purchase option do not by themselves establish separate leases where the deed otherwise treats the property as one demise and does not specify a distinct area for a separate land lease. Under the Act's definitions, a composite lease of a building with appurtenant land does not confer the rights in sections 3 or 9.

predicates.tenant_seeks_statutory_protection_in_eje: A tenant facing an ejectment suit claims statutory protection based on the lease.
predicates.deed_covers_building_and_land: The lease deed covers both a building and land.
predicates.deed_treats_premises_as_one_demise: The deed provides for the building and land to be held under a single lease arrangement, including common term and termination provisions.
predicates.no_separately_defined_land_area: The deed does not identify and delineate an area of land as the subject of a distinct lease.

issues.definition: When a tenant claims statutory protection in an ejectment proceeding under a deed covering a building and land that treats them as one demise without defining a separate land area, the lease is an indivisible composite lease.

issues.legal_issue: A customary lease clause permitting removal of structures does not, without more, establish an intention to deny compensation or avoid statutory tenant protection.
material_facts: The lease permitted the tenant to remove structures at the end of the lease.
The clause did not state that the tenant would receive no compensation for structures.
The Court found that such a removal clause was usual in leases and that the tenant's right to remove structures would exist even without the clause.
issues.conclusion: The removal clause did not establish that the parties intended to deny compensation or avoid the statutory protection.
issues.legal_principle: In considering the lease under the Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, a normal clause concerning removal of structures is not evidence of an intention to exclude statutory rights when it says nothing about compensation. The Court noted the context of section 12, including the retrospective deletion of its proviso, and that the lease clause merely addressed removal, a position that would otherwise follow in law under the Transfer of Property Act.

predicates.lease_has_removal_only_clause: The lease permits the tenant to remove structures at the end of the lease.
predicates.clause_omits_compensation_disclaimer: The removal clause does not state that the tenant is disentitled to compensation for structures.

issues.definition: When a tenant claims statutory protection in an ejectment proceeding and the lease contains only a customary removal clause with no compensation disclaimer, that clause does not establish an intent to avoid the protection.
